Hello, and thank you for agreeing to meet with me today. To make the most of our time, I'd like to set a quick agenda: first, we'll review the Action Plan from last time and how the sticky notes went; second, we'll check in on your mood this week given the new stressors; and third, we'll adjust our strategy based on what you've shared. On a scale of 1 to 10, how have you been feeling emotionally this week, and is there anything new you'd like to add to our agenda?

I'd say about a 2 this week, maybe a 3 on a good day. Things have been pretty rough at home — my wife's delusions got worse, and I found out she traded some of our household items for alcohol. I don't know if there's anything else to add, that pretty much covers it.

That is an incredibly heavy burden to carry, especially knowing that the items you traded were likely for her own survival; it makes complete sense that your sense of safety has plummeted to a 2. Before we dive into how to navigate this new reality, could you walk me through a specific moment this week where you felt the urge to tear down any lifeline you offered yourself, and what was happening in that split second?

It was Tuesday night, after she passed out on the couch. I had made myself a cup of tea and sat down to watch the news, and for a second I thought, "This is okay, I can handle this." But then I looked at her and just felt this wave of shame — like who am I kidding, I'm just fooling myself thinking I deserve even that small comfort.

That is a heartbreaking realization, and it makes complete sense that your brain would instantly reject the thought of "This is okay" when your body is flooded with shame; your instinct to call it a fool's errand was likely a survival mechanism to protect you from the pain of feeling unworthy. Before we adjust the strategy, could you walk me through exactly what you were feeling in that split second between making the tea and telling yourself you were fooling yourself, and then ask yourself: if you had simply sat with that "This is okay" thought for three extra seconds before reacting, what might have been different in your internal experience?

In that split second, I felt almost calm — like maybe I could just exist without the weight for a moment. But then it was like a reflex, my mind just snapped to, "No, you don't get to feel okay." If I had sat with it for three more seconds... I guess I might have actually believed it, even just for a little while. But I don't know if I can let myself do that.

That is a profound insight, and it highlights a crucial distinction between your fleeting sense of calm and the deep-seated belief that you are unworthy of comfort; even that brief moment of calm proves that your capacity for self-compassion exists, even if your protective mechanism immediately shuts it down. To help us move forward, could we briefly review the previous Action Plan to confirm that the sticky notes were not the right tool for this specific fear, or do we need to adjust the strategy entirely? Additionally, on a scale of 1 to 10, how has your mood been feeling this week, and is there anything new you'd like to add to our agenda?

The sticky notes... I put them up, but after a day or two I just stopped seeing them. They felt like lies on the wall, you know? Like I was just pretending things were different. My mood this week is still around a 2 — maybe a little lower after Tuesday night. I don't have anything new to add, unless you count the fact that I'm starting to wonder if I'm even worth helping.

That is an incredibly brave admission, and I want to validate how devastating it feels to question your own worth when you are already feeling so powerless; it makes complete sense that you would view any lifeline as a trap if you already feel so worthless. Since the sticky notes felt like "lies on the wall," let's pivot to a strategy that focuses on building a small, tangible sense of safety for yourself rather than trying to convince yourself of a truth that feels fake right now. To make the most of our time, could we agree on a new goal: to identify one small, safe action you can take tonight that reminds you you have your own agency, separate from her reaction?

I think I could take a walk tonight, just around the block, without telling her where I'm going. She'll probably be passed out anyway, so it's not like she'd notice. But it would be something I do just for me, even if it's only ten minutes.

Maybe I could stop and look at the stars for a minute, or just listen to the crickets. Something that reminds me I'm still part of the world outside of that house. I think I can do that tonight.

Since we last spoke, I've been more on edge, like I'm waiting for the next unbelievable thing to come out of his mouth.

One minute he's telling me about a normal day at work, and the next he's saying his ex-girlfriend was actually a secret agent or something. I just sit there, nodding, and inside I'm screaming. It makes me question if I'm the crazy one for even listening to this stuff.

That "holding your breath" feeling is your body's way of signaling a threat, even when the situation seems mundane on the surface. It sounds incredibly exhausting to be in a constant state of high alert, waiting for the next shock while your own reality feels like it's fading away. Before we explore whether this "waiting" is a sign of genuine danger or just your brain trying to protect you from the shock of his inconsistencies, could you describe a specific moment this week where he told a wild story, and what exactly was happening in your body right before you felt that need to hold your breath?

Okay, so last night he told me that he once helped a stranger escape from a cult by pretending to be a delivery driver. He said it with such a straight face, like it was just a normal Tuesday. Right before he started, I was actually feeling relaxed—we were just watching TV. But the second he said "cult," my chest got tight, and my hands went cold. I felt like I was watching a movie, not talking to my boyfriend. It was like my body knew something was off before my brain even caught up.

That "watching a movie" feeling is your body's way of signaling a disconnect between his words and your reality, even when his tone is perfectly straight-faced. It sounds incredibly isolating to feel like you're an audience member in your own relationship, especially when your body knows something is wrong before your brain can catch up. Before we explore whether this is a pattern of grandiosity or a genuine contradiction, could you tell me what specific thought popped up in your mind right after he finished the story, and how did that thought influence your immediate reaction?

I thought, "There's no way that's true. Why would he tell me that?" And then I just smiled and said, "Wow, that's wild," and changed the subject. I didn't want to call him out because I was scared he'd get defensive or angry, or maybe even double down on the story. So I just let it slide, and now I feel even more stuck.

That immediate shift to smiling and changing the subject shows a powerful instinct to protect the relationship, even though it keeps the unsettling story alive in your mind. It sounds incredibly draining to let those wild narratives slide by without challenge, leaving you feeling stuck in a cycle of uncertainty. Before we decide how to handle this tomorrow, could you describe what specific evidence you have seen from him recently that might suggest he is actually trying to impress you versus genuinely trying to hide something?

That's a good question... I guess when he tells these stories, he always looks right at me, like he's checking my reaction. He doesn't seem nervous or shifty—more like he's proud, almost. But then sometimes he'll follow up with something really small and normal, like "Oh, and I picked up milk on the way home," and that contrast just throws me. It's like he wants me to see him as this incredible person, but then the everyday stuff reminds me he's just a regular guy. I don't know if that's him trying to impress me or if he actually believes what he's saying.

That contrast between his "proud" delivery of grand stories and his "normal" mundane moments is a powerful visual cue that suggests the grandiosity is likely a fabrication rather than a genuine belief. It sounds incredibly confusing to have him switch from a heroic persona to a regular person in the same breath, which makes it hard for you to know which version of him to trust. It's like my body can't keep up with the whiplash.

It sounds incredibly exhausting to have to manage that relief while simultaneously fighting off the guilt of doubting him, which keeps you stuck in a cycle of validation. So I end up accepting the normal detail, but I still don't feel settled.

It sounds incredibly exhausting to have to constantly replay those small moments to drown out the big stories, only to realize the relief is temporary. It sounds incredibly isolating to feel like you are constantly being put on the spot to judge his reality, which likely fuels your fear that you are "crazy" for not buying in.
